newsitem.title: TUNISIA: FOCUS-Tunisia to issue $3.3 billion bonds by 2001.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Tunisia to issue $3.3 billion bonds by 2001.

text.p: Tunisia plans to launch 10 and 15-year bond issues on the international markets totalling 3.040 billion dinars ($3.313 billion) between 1997 and 2001, an official report showed on Thursday.

The report on financings needed by the 9th Development Plan 1997-2001 obtained by Reuters showed that in addition, Tunisia plans to seek syndicated loans totalling 600 million dinars ($654 million) during the same period.

This puts the total to be borrowed on the financial markets at 3.64 billion dinars of which some 660 million dinars are to be contracted by the local banks between 1997 and 2001, and the remainder by the Tunisian state, the report showed.

Tunisia started looking at international capital markets in 1994 because international development agencies found that it had reached a degree of development which made it non-eligible for concessional loans.

Since then, it successfully offered five Samurai bonds totalling 985 million dinars on the Japanese market for a five to 15-year maturity, and three syndicated loans on the London place worth 460 million dinars.

On Thursday, Standard & Poor's assigned its triple-B'-minus long-term rating to the Republic of Tunisia and the central Bank of Tunisia's foreign currency-denominated debt. The agency has assigned Tunisia a short-term foreign currency credit rating of A-3'.
In addition, Standard and Poor's assigned its single A-' long-term and A-1' short-term ratings to the Republic's dinar-denominated debt.

It said the outlook on the ratings was stable and that these ratings reflected solid public finance, a conservative monetary policy track record, a moderate external debt and debt service, gradual removal of price, trade, credit and labor market distorsions.
Standard & Poors says that the country's outlook was stable and that Tunisian President Zine al-Abidine Ben Ali "likely will consolidate reforms in the medium term."

"However, the benefits of reform probably will materialize only slowly, particularly if large-scale privatization and deregulation are postponed. Inprovements in credit worthiness hinge mainly on the pace at which the state reduces its economic role," it added.
Previous ratings were BBB+ by the Japan Bond Reserach Institute (JBRI), BBB3 by Moody's, and BBB-minus for the long term and A3 for the short term by IBCA.
Tunisia forecasts also to get credit lines facilities totalling 910 million dinars during the same period through bilateral trade agreements, the Tunisian government report says.

Other external financings for Tunisian development and reform projects between 1997 and 2001 will come through loans or donations totalling 4.55 billion dinars from the World Bank, the European Union and its subsidiary European Investment Bank, and the African Development Bank, the report says.

The donations would amount 750 million dinars and would come from the E.U. to support the modernisation of the Tunisian economy to help it adapt to a free trade zone agreement Tunisia signed with it in 1995.

The report forecasts that Tunisia's external debt as a proportion of gross domestic product (GDP) would drop to 40.8 percent in 2001 from 51.5 percent in 1996, and the debt servicing ratio to the current receipts would also fall to 16.2 percent from 18.3 percent in 1996. ($=1.09 dinar)
